summary: Ordinal numbers are adjectives. From three to ten they are built on the root of the number with the pattern فَاعِل: ثَلَاثَة → ثَالِث “third”, أَرْبَعَة → رَابِع, خَمْسَة → خَامِس … عَشَرَة → عَاشِر. “Second” is ثَانٍ (definite الثَّانِي), and “first” is a word of its own, أَوَّل, feminine أُولَى. Unlike the cardinals 3–10 they have no gender polarity: they follow the noun and agree with it in gender, case and definiteness like any adjective — الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ “the third day”, السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ “the third hour = three o’clock”. “Last” is الْأَخِير after the noun (or آخِر before it, in a construct). Dates: الْيَوْمُ هُوَ الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو “today is the fifth of May” — the masculine ordinal (for الْيَوْم) + مِنْ + the month; “on” is فِي + genitive: فِي الْخَامِسِ مِنْ مَايُو. The clock: السَّاعَةُ + the feminine ordinal, with وَالنِّصْفُ “half past”, وَالرُّبْعُ “a quarter past” and إِلَّا رُبْعًا “a quarter to”; one o’clock is السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ. Centuries take ordinals too: الْقَرْنُ الْعَاشِرُ.

blocks.caption: From three on the ordinal is the root of the number on the pattern فَاعِل; “first” and “second” are special (أَوَّل; ثَانٍ from the root of اِثْنَان).

blocks.title: Ordinals agree, cardinals reverse.
blocks.text: ثَلَاثَةُ أَيَّامٍ “three days” (the number looks feminine with a masculine noun) — but الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ “the third day” (masculine with masculine), السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ “the third hour” (feminine with feminine). The ordinal is an ordinary adjective after its noun.

blocks.title: ثَانٍ is defective.
blocks.text: Indefinite ثَانٍ (nominative and genitive), ثَانِيًا (accusative); definite الثَّانِي (nominative and genitive), الثَّانِيَ (accusative): فِي الطَّابِقِ الثَّانِي “on the second floor”. The feminine ثَانِيَة / الثَّانِيَة is regular.

head: time
Arabic
blocks.caption: The clock: السَّاعَةُ + the feminine ordinal (the hour is feminine). One o’clock uses the cardinal الْوَاحِدَةُ; eleven and twelve are compound ordinals. Minutes are added with وَ: وَعِشْرُونَ دَقِيقَةً.

blocks.title: Half past, quarter past, quarter to.
blocks.text: وَالنِّصْفُ “and the half”: الثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ = 3:30 (half past the hour just gone); وَالرُّبْعُ “and the quarter” = a quarter past; إِلَّا رُبْعًا “less a quarter” = a quarter to: الرَّابِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا = 3:45.

blocks.title: “At what time?”
blocks.text: “At” is فِي (or عِنْدَ) + the genitive: فِي السَّاعَةِ السَّادِسَةِ “at six o’clock”. Asking: فِي أَيِّ سَاعَةٍ؟ “at what time?” or simply مَتَى؟ — and “what time is it?” is كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟

head: Arabic
meaning
rows: Today is the fifth of May.
عِيدُ مِيلَادِي فِي الْأَوَّلِ مِنْ يَنَايِرَ.
My birthday is on the first of January.
We arrived on the second of May.
We will travel on the tenth of August.
blocks.caption: Dates: the masculine ordinal (agreeing with an understood الْيَوْم “the day”) + مِنْ + the month; with فِي the ordinal is genitive.

blocks.title: Above ten.
blocks.text: 11th الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ (f. الْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ), 12th الثَّانِيَ عَشَرَ (f. الثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ), 13th الثَّالِثَ عَشَرَ …; from 20 on the ordinal is the cardinal with the article: الْعِشْرُونَ “the twentieth”, الْحَادِي وَالْعِشْرُونَ “the twenty-first”: الْقَرْنُ الْحَادِي وَالْعِشْرُونَ.

blocks.title: Fractions are nouns.
blocks.text: نِصْف “half”, ثُلُث “a third”, رُبْع “a quarter” (from the same roots as the numbers) stand before what they divide, in a construct: نِصْفُ سَاعَةٍ “half an hour”, رُبْعُ سَاعَةٍ “a quarter of an hour”, نِصْفُ الْعَصِيرِ “half the juice”.

Written dates usually have digits (5/5/2026); read aloud, formal Arabic says the ordinal (الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو), while everyday speech often says the cardinal. The month names have two series (مَايُو / أَيَّار, lesson 15); the Hijri calendar has its own months.

askYourself: Is it a rank (first, second …) or a count (one, two …)? A rank → the ordinal, an adjective after the noun.
Is the noun masculine or feminine? The ordinal agrees (no polarity): الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ / السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ.
Does the noun have the article? Then the ordinal has it too: الْبَيْتُ الثَّالِثُ (but بَيْتٌ ثَالِثٌ “a third house”).
Is it “first” or “second”? → أَوَّل / أُولَى; ثَانٍ / الثَّانِي / الثَّانِيَة (defective in the masculine).
A clock time? → السَّاعَةُ + feminine ordinal (+ وَالنِّصْفُ / وَالرُّبْعُ / إِلَّا رُبْعًا); one o’clock is الْوَاحِدَةُ.
A date? → masculine ordinal + مِنْ + month; “on” = فِي + genitive.

traps: No polarity with ordinals: الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ (not *الثَّالِثَةُ) — only the cardinals 3–10 take the “opposite” form.
One o’clock is السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ, not *الْأُولَى.
ثَانٍ is defective: الثَّانِي in the nominative and genitive, الثَّانِيَ in the accusative.
أَوَّلُ + an indefinite noun is “the first …”: أَوَّلُ يَوْمٍ; أَوَّلُ الْيَوْمِ (with the article) is “the beginning of the day”.
“Half past three” counts from the hour that has passed: الثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ = 3:30.
آخِر “last” and آخَر “other” differ in one vowel: آخِرُ يَوْمٍ “the last day” / يَوْمٌ آخَرُ “another day”.

quiz.why: The ordinal agrees like an adjective: masculine with الْيَوْم; no polarity.
For one o’clock Arabic uses the feminine cardinal, not the ordinal.
إِلَّا رُبْعًا “less a quarter”: four less a quarter.
ثَانٍ is defective: the definite genitive is الثَّانِي, with no vowel on the ي.

quiz.q: “the first time” — which is NOT correct?
quiz.why: After a feminine noun “first” is أُولَى; before the noun the construct أَوَّلُ مَرَّةٍ is also right.

quiz.q: Today is the fifth of May:
quiz.why: Formal Arabic uses the masculine ordinal (for الْيَوْم) + مِنْ + the month.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew ordinals 1–10 are adjectives on a pattern with -i (שְׁלִישִׁי “third”, feminine שְׁלִישִׁית); above ten Hebrew uses cardinals, Arabic keeps ordinals (الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ).

German ordinals also agree (der dritte Tag, die dritte Stunde) and dates use them (der fünfte Mai); but the clock uses cardinals (um drei Uhr), and halb vier is 3:30, where Arabic says الثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ.
Chinese makes ordinals with 第 (第三天) and writes dates from big to small (五月五日); Arabic puts the day first: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو.
The cardinals 3–10 take the opposite gender (ثَلَاثَةُ أَيَّامٍ); the ordinals simply agree (الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ).

notes.text: Greek ordinals are adjectives that agree too (τρίτος, τρίτη); the Greek clock uses cardinals (στις τρεις), while Arabic uses the feminine ordinal: فِي السَّاعَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ.

Russian ordinals agree like adjectives (третий день, третья неделя), as in Arabic; Russian names the hour in progress with an ordinal (пятый час = after four), while Arabic’s الْخَامِسَةُ is five o’clock exactly.
Spanish ordinals agree (primero, primera), but dates use cardinals (el cinco de mayo); formal Arabic uses the ordinal: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو.
English adds -th to the number; Arabic builds 3rd–10th from the root on one pattern (ثَالِث، رَابِع، خَامِس) and makes them agree in gender: الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ / السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ.
French dates use cardinals except the first (le premier mai, le cinq mai); Arabic uses ordinals for every day (الْأَوَّلُ مِنْ مَايُو، الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو).

German ordinals agree (der dritte Tag, die dritte Stunde) and dates use them (der fünfte Mai), as in Arabic; the clock differs: um drei Uhr, and halb vier = 3:30, whereas Arabic says الثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ.
Hindi has special words for the first ordinals (पहला, दूसरा, तीसरा, चौथा, छठा) and -वाँ for the rest (पाँचवाँ); Arabic forms 3rd–10th regularly on فَاعِل and has special words only for 1st and 2nd.
Persian adds -om to the cardinal (سوم “third”, پنجم “fifth”); Arabic changes the word itself on the pattern فَاعِل (ثَالِث، خَامِس).
Marathi has special words for the first ordinals (पहिला, दुसरा, तिसरा, चौथा) and -वा after (पाचवा); in Arabic only “first” and “second” are irregular.
Hebrew ordinals 1–10 are adjectives too, with -i (שְׁלִישִׁי “third”, רְבִיעִי “fourth”), and agree in gender; above ten Hebrew uses cardinals, while Arabic keeps ordinals (الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ).
Turkish adds -(I)ncI to the cardinal (üçüncü “third”), and the clock and dates use cardinals (saat üç, beş mayıs); Arabic uses ordinals for both.
Japanese makes ordinals with 第 or -番目 (三番目) and says the hour with a cardinal + 時 (三時); Arabic uses the feminine ordinal: السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ.
Korean uses 째 / 번째 for ordinals (셋째, 세 번째) and native cardinals for the hour (세 시); Arabic uses the feminine ordinal for the hour.
Finnish ordinals agree in case and number (kolmas, kolmannen) and dates use them (viides toukokuuta); the clock uses cardinals (kello kolme), while Arabic uses the ordinal.
Hungarian adds -dik (harmadik, ötödik) and says dates with a day form (május ötödike); Arabic uses the ordinal adjective after the noun (الْيَوْمُ الْخَامِسُ).

Swahili forms ordinals with -a + the number (siku ya tatu “the third day”) and counts the hours from sunrise (saa moja = seven o’clock); Arabic has a special ordinal form that agrees in gender, and its clock starts at midnight and noon.
Luganda, like Swahili, counts clock hours from sunrise (essaawa emu = seven o’clock); Arabic counts from midnight and noon: السَّاعَةُ السَّابِعَةُ = seven o’clock.
Chinese makes ordinals with 第 (第三天) and writes dates from big to small (五月五日); Arabic puts the day first: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَايُو.
Vietnamese puts thứ before the number (thứ ba “third” — also Tuesday) and dates go day–month (ngày 5 tháng 5); Arabic uses an ordinal adjective after the noun.
Inuktitut “first” is sivulliq, “the one in front”, a word of its own; Arabic “first”, أَوَّل, is also not built from “one”, while 3rd–10th follow one pattern (ثَالِث … عَاشِر).
